systems.name: Numbers on a line, and the one question they cannot answer
systems.summary: The ordinary numbers as places on a line, adding as sliding and multiplying as stretching or flipping, and the question no place on the line answers

blocks.label: Adding slides
blocks.note: Every number moves the same distance the same way

blocks.label: Multiplying stretches, and by a negative number flips
blocks.note: Times two doubles every distance from zero; times minus one turns the whole line round through zero

blocks.label: The question
blocks.tex: x^{2} = -1 \quad \text{has no } x \text{ on the line}
blocks.note: A number times itself is never below zero: the page tries every x and draws the square, and it never dips under the axis

dimension.label: What is missing
dimension.note: Flipping is what minus one does. The question asks for half a flip, and the line has no room for it

systems.name: What 𝑖 is
systems.summary: Minus one is a half turn about zero; so half of that is a quarter turn, and a number that turns by a quarter is what i is. Done twice it is a half turn, which is minus one

blocks.label: The definition
blocks.note: Not a trick and not a mystery: a quarter turn followed by a quarter turn is a half turn, and a half turn is multiplying by minus one

blocks.label: Going round
blocks.note: The page multiplies by 𝑖 again and again and the arrow turns a quarter each time, back where it started after four

blocks.label: A second axis
blocks.note: A number is now a place in a plane: a along the old line, b along the new one. The old numbers are the ones with b equal to zero

dimension.label: The name
dimension.note: A name from the seventeenth century, given as an insult and kept by habit. Nothing on that axis is less real than a length

systems.name: Complex numbers: adding
systems.summary: Each number an arrow from zero; to add two, put the second arrow's tail on the first one's tip. The parts add separately and never mix

blocks.label: Adding
blocks.note: The along part and the up part each add on their own. The page walks the second arrow out from the first's tip

blocks.label: Subtracting
blocks.note: The same walk with the second arrow turned round

blocks.label: The length
blocks.note: How far the arrow reaches: Pythagoras on its two parts. Two arrows' lengths do not add unless they point the same way

dimension.label: What adding does not do
dimension.note: Adding never turns anything. The turning is all in multiplying, on the next page

systems.name: Complex numbers: multiplying
systems.summary: To multiply two arrows, add their angles and multiply their lengths. The page turns and stretches one arrow into the product while the reader watches

blocks.label: The four terms
blocks.note: Multiply out as with any two brackets; the one term with 𝑖 times 𝑖 in it is minus one, which is where the minus in ac minus bd comes from

blocks.label: What that is, as a picture
blocks.note: Lengths multiply, angles add. The page shows the product arrow reached by turning the first by the second's angle and stretching by its length

blocks.label: Multiplying by i again
blocks.note: So times 𝑖 is a quarter turn with no stretch, which is the last page's definition read from this page's rule

dimension.label: Length and angle name the number as well as the two parts do
dimension.note: Two ways to say where an arrow points; the page shows both for every arrow it draws

systems.name: Which points stay?
systems.summary: Start at zero, square and add c, again and again. For some values of c the path stays near zero for ever, for others it runs away. The values of c that stay form the Mandelbrot set

blocks.label: One squaring
blocks.note: Multiplying a number by itself: the angle adds to itself, the length multiplies by itself

blocks.label: Square and add c
blocks.note: Square, then slide by c, every step. The page draws these points as the path from zero

blocks.label: The Mandelbrot set
blocks.note: Every c whose path never passes length two. The page fills these in

dimension.label: The escape test
dimension.note: Once the length passes two the square outruns c for ever, which is how the page decides that a path has left

systems.name: Euler's formula
systems.summary: The growth curve from topic 3, given an imaginary rate, does not grow: it goes round the unit circle at a steady pace, and its two shadows are the cosine and the sine

blocks.label: Euler's formula
blocks.note: The point on the unit circle at angle theta. The page runs theta round and draws the two shadows as waves beside it

blocks.label: Why it goes round
blocks.note: The rate of change is the position turned a quarter: always sideways, never outward, which is what moving on a circle means

blocks.label: The famous case
blocks.note: Half a turn lands on minus one. The page stops there and says so

dimension.label: Where this is used next
dimension.note: The sinusoidal position vectors of topic 4 are this formula at many speeds, and the swing of topic 2 is its real shadow

systems.name: Quaternions
systems.summary: Hamilton's numbers with three imaginary units, a unit one being a turn in space; two turns in a different order land differently, so the numbers do not commute

blocks.label: Hamilton's rule, 1843
blocks.tex: i^{2} = j^{2} = k^{2} = ijk = -1, \qquad ij = k,\ ji = -k
blocks.note: Three imaginary units instead of one. The second line follows from the first and is the whole difference from the plane: the order of a product matters

blocks.label: A turn as a quaternion
blocks.tex: q = \cos\tfrac{\theta}{2} + \sin\tfrac{\theta}{2}\,(u_{x} i + u_{y} j + u_{z} k)
blocks.note: The turn by theta about the unit axis u. Half the angle goes in, which is why a full turn is minus one and two full turns are one

blocks.label: Turning a point
blocks.note: The point as a quaternion with no real part, sandwiched. In the plane the sandwich collapses to one multiplication, because there the order never mattered

blocks.label: Two turns
blocks.note: First q1 then q2 is the product q2 q1. The page draws both orders at once, and the two houses end facing different ways

blocks.label: The path between two orientations
blocks.note: Shoemake, 1985: the shortest smooth turn from a to b, used by every game engine and by the run on this page

dimension.label: Only three such systems
dimension.note: Frobenius, 1878: the reals, the complex numbers and the quaternions are the only finite systems over the reals in which every non-zero number divides. The octonions follow by losing associativity too

definitions.name: The complex plane
definitions.note: Every number is a place, or an arrow from zero to that place. The old number line is the horizontal axis

definitions.name: Length and angle
definitions.note: How far the arrow reaches and which way it points. Multiplying works on these two; adding works on the parts

definitions.name: The mirror image
definitions.note: The same arrow reflected in the horizontal axis; a number times its mirror image is a plain length squared
